searchText: I pinned a couple of others for people who want to get caught up to speed. If you see any others, or I if I miss something let me know. And if any of the pinned authors want to update their statements happy to unpin or pin another or remove them all. 😄 if the EIP in question is part of a bigger EVM overhaul, is there a chance that it could still go into a future fork along with related EIPS? Yes, we could very easily add it to a future fork, the work is already done. It is more work now to disable it (bit of work) and test that all clients are still in consensus for everything else but the EIP (medium amount of work). perhaps <@!683653554631868440> would feel better knowing that the effort wouldn't have gone to waste but simply delayed then I'm not sure we can guarantee that, though I can understand the need to be extra careful about what goes in as it is easier for features to be added than to be removed but i understand <@!683653554631868440> 's frustration Yeah, on that last point, I do think it's worth thinking about the second-order effects a bit. Removing the change may be beneficial from a technical PoV, but it's really not great to have people spend years working on something, "think it's in" and have it removed at the last minute. It also does affect the perception of "Ethereum governance" to remove something at the last minute without a very strong rationale to do so (ex: a security risk). I'm not saying we shouldn't do it, but I do think the second order effects here are potentially more consequential than whether 2315 is in or not: will people want to take on working on large EIPs? How will this change user expectations w.r.t. Ethereum, especially larger "commerical" users like dapps, infrastructure, etc. Is there anything that can be added to the EIP process that makes it less likely for this sort of thing to happen? Like making it a requirement for affected parties to be present at a Core Dev Call? Yes, we will definitely do that I don't think we necessarily need them to come to AllCoreDevs. We did it async for 1559, for example: https://github.com/ethereum-cat-herders/1559-outreach (modulo the contentious aspect, which we did do async). Could this have been avoided if the solidity team saw the EIP earlier or had they already seen it but only recently came to light that it would not in fact be useful? Yes, I think there are two things we probably should do: 1. Make it part of the EIP process/template to explicitly highlight who wants this and why 2. Make it part of the ACD process to communicate these changes more broadly earlier on, and potentially catalog objections better. One challenge with (2) is that people opposing generally just want to share their objection once and move on, while champions are willing to keep pushing their EIP "forever", and have a much higher incentive to keep engaging, in almost all cases, than critics (unless they are _very_ negatively affected). For that reason, I feel like EIPs should require the champion to convince others to use the EIP before it can be considered for inclusion. This doesn't work for every core EIP (like 2929), but for things like 2315 and 3074 it is a good baseline to show that the EIP does have proponents who plan to use the EIP on a large scale once it is deployed. The Solidity team has been aware of and participated in EIP-2315 since long before it was proposed. I would like to see their most recent analysis. And my intemperate "bullshit" is just that we are at the very last stage of deploying an upgrade. EIP-2315 has been planned for this upgrade for many months now. It just isn't the time to be asking EIP authors (for any EIP) to re-justify their work. The only relevant questions at this point are, "has it been implemented?", "has it been tested?", and "is it broken?". Like I've said all along, it is very unfortunate that we've found ourselves in this situation, but we are here now. We should make the best decision with the current information and it looks like most agree that given the solidity team does not find this EIP useful and that there are no other projects which plan to use subroutines in the near future, the best decision is to remove the EIP from Berlin. Those really are the only questions I consider relevant at this point. The time for the questions you raise has passed. I'm not joking. You said previously that it is up to the critics to convince core devs to abandon the EIP, and assuming we can use the same fork blocks without 2315, it appears they agree to abandon the EIP for Berlin. There is an unfortunate chicken and egg problem here I don't readily see a solution for. People don't build things that require core changes because they don't think it is possible to get them in at all, or in a reasonable time. Or that, having achieved consensus at getting them in, the consensus process can be re-opened for any reason up until the very last moment. At this point - and I'm still feeling rather intemperate - I would not care to participate in further core EIPs - or encourage others to submit them. All pain, no gain. And further discussion should probably go here rather than clutter this channel. https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/263 The meta-discussion that I do think this raises here is procedural. At what point in the process of an upgrade can certain decisions be considered done with? People make plans and spend money based on the decisions we announce. I still submit that we are at the point that the relevant questions are - "has it been implemented?", "has it been tested?", and "is it broken?" 1) improve EIP process 2) defer static analysis work for future fork 3) keep berlin on schedule = my 2c EDIT: See most recent message where I change my mind: https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/745077610685661265/816575516907798539 Just caught up on everything. This is a very unfortunate situation and there isn't a good answer. My thoughts: - a lot of things need to be improved process wise, especially the things <@!683653554631868440> mentioned about when to cut off changes. - I do think there is new information in that members of the Solidity team, including their lead, are not in favor of this EIP and multiple people (including myself) were under the impression they were on board when they weren't. That is in part the fault of the Solidity team for choosing not to take part in a process that decides these things. - If it were just the fact that the Solidity team didn't think it would be beneficial that would be one thing, but now there is an unanswered question about who will use it. I like what <@!211091239112671234> said: > Agree it's wonky to remove last minute. It's sooo bad, and I can't understand why ppl wake up now to sth that's been planned for such a long time. I mean ffs. > However, adding another dead-on-arrival feature is also pretty useless. > Nothing is temporary, anything added is there forever. So if it's not useful, it's a lot better to never have had it Although we are doing a bad thing in doing very last minute changes, it would be worse imo to have an unused feature which the Solidity team seems to think will not help things. For this reason I'm personally leaning towards removing it and pushing back the Ropsten fork a bit. I feel for Greg's position and acknowledge all the hard work that was put into this EIP. It really sucks we are having to deal with this. I think it would be different if there were more people than Greg advocating for this loudly and if it wasn't the Solidity team with objections. Removing it last minute will set a bad ecosystem example and deter people from working on EIPs (at least in the short term). However, leaving it in on principle to follow a broken process that will be improved over time doesn't feel right when multiple people believe, at minimum, it will introduce tech. debt. I don't think people recognize how bad the precedent is. One more thing that got cut out while I was copy/pasting: <@683653554631868440> I want to respectfully ask that you have more professional decorum. You've requested the same of people like Ameen on ACD calls and I think the same should apply to venues like this. You refused to answer people's questions and called bullshit on people who are trying to figure this out and get questions answered in good faith. I think we should all hold ourselves to high standards when communicating, even when tensions are high. I believe precedents can be reversed. This process/system is very broken right now in multiple ways and I believe incremental improvements will help. I still believe tech. debt and having features that a prominent EVM related team is saying is bad to add trumps the principle of not making changes after a cut-off date in this instance. The precedent is that the Core Devs cannot be trusted to carry through with their announced decisions. Because we don't. How many times do you think we can walk that back? (I apologize for the cursing.) Not sure. A factor that may influence that is the merge and how Eth2 dev process combines and influences the process we currently have. I don't think there's a way to know. One thing we do know is that tech. debt can be more accurately measured and can be forever. Some debt is smaller than others. Three very simple instructions that Solidity doesn't need but others teams want seem worth it, especially when they have already withstood months of discussion, implementation and testing. This was under the guise that Solidity team would be one of the primary users of it right? Who are the other people/teams saying they would use it? No such guise, though until today I had no reason to believe they wouldn't. Again - they are basic primitives for most every other machine I know of - but I'm discussing that on <@543900561460822016>'s issue. Can you link to it again? https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/263 On this channel it's the precedent I'm concerned with, and the appropriateness of raising this sort of objection so late in our process. I don't see a strong enough technical argument here to make it worth setting such a bad precedent. It might be good to hear from the Vyper team if we can. Thanks for mentioning some of the teams who would use it in the thread <@683653554631868440>, that helps. I just spoke with Bryant, and he confirmed his interest on Twitter. Will invite him here. Ugh, I really don't like the idea of bumping the gas limit after Berlin. While we fix the attack vector, we haven't fixed the state growth problem. https://twitter.com/fubuloubu/status/1366949333854277632?s=21 Seemed relevant Why am I always asleep for the best debates. 😢 But surely because the consequences of state growth are delayed, we don't strictly need a state fix now, rather we just need a _commitment_ to a state fix now? which is something I fully support btw (see my post on magicians today) If we had a concrete plan, roadmap, and timeline for state growth reduction I would agree. https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/weak-statelessness-and-or-state-expiry-coming-soon/5453 However, right now we have a vague plan, a fuzzy roadmap, and no timeline. I think now is basically the time to start solidifying the plan 😆 One thing we have to decide at some point is whether to prioritize weak statelessness or state expiry And *once* that plan is solidified and we have teams *committed* to working on it I would favor a block size increase. 🙂 What I'm concerned about is that it will be 3-5 years before we actually implement a stateless plan, and that is a lot of time for state growth. So we have a mini-team (Guillaume, with Dankrad and myself advising) working on a Verkle tree implementation, and the regenesis people have been working on state expiry I think we're ~1-1.5 years away if we put our feet down and say "X is the solution, we're doing it" This is in the context of our (Ethereum community's) historic sluggishness (for good reason) on implementing major changes (like Proof of Stake for examp
